continuity-g7bty0.name: Continuity
continuity-g7bty0.summary: Wiki facts rot silently: nobody edited the page, the world just moved. Continuity re-checks each fact against the live web and drafts the fix for a maintainer to approve.

inspiration_intel.the_wedge: They assumed the expensive step (generation, review, data entry) should be priced before it runs.
inspiration_intel.what_it_does: Wiki facts rot silently: nobody edited the page, the world just moved. Continuity re-checks each fact against the live web and drafts the fix for a maintainer to approve.
steal_this: Invert the pipeline: generate last, verify first. Ship the checker as the artifact and the content as its output.
Anything the architecture can enforce, the architecture enforces. Probabilistic components get proposals; deterministic components get verdicts.
Find the metric practitioners already eyeball, instrument it, and ship the delta. A number turns a vibe into a product.
inspiration_intel.naive_version_vs_this: A demo that needs the user to already know what to type. — then Continuity made the step measurable, gated, or priced instead.
inspiration_intel.reuse_surface: portable to any tool with an expensive generation step

audit.worth_note: The diagnosis is worth more than the demo: a fact that used to be true and quietly stopped being true looks exactly like every correct sentence around it, and nobody edited the page — the world moved on. Treating wiki rot as a decay problem with a per-claim due date instead of an error problem is the right shape, and keeping the human as writer of record (a cited diff, never a publish) is the right posture for public knowledge infrastructure. The write-up also documents its own development discipline in the same breath as the product, which lets a reader check the cost claim against the fixture claim.

artifact_exists.why: no source repo linked, but the page publishes a working artifact: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gzsIQCyKa9k

build_is_real.why: no repository published, so the build cannot be read

limits_disclosed.why: the challenges section discloses operating constraints (what the pipeline costs to run and to iterate on), but no accuracy, coverage or failure-mode limit; the future-work section implies the remaining open edges

numbers_add_up.why: 1 figure(s) we re-derived do not match the page: 'run all six stages end to end' versus the seven numbered steps in the feature walkthrough — internally inconsistent as written: the user-visible walkthrough enumerates read, prioritise, research, judge, write edit, cross-check and hand back (seven), while the cost narrative says six stages — consistent only if the stage count is the implementation's and the steps are the narrative's, which the page never states

stack_consistency.why: no repo to cross-check the declared stack against

test_or_eval_evidence.why: a harness is described (fixture) but no result, run link or case count is published, so it cannot be checked

assumptions: a wiki or knowledge base with a review workflow you can post diffs into (MediaWiki pending changes, or a PR-style flow)
a per-claim research budget, since a pass costs a search plus several model calls for every claim on the page
a decision about contested facts: staff the disagreement bucket, or suppress that category rather than flood maintainers
clone_cost.estimate: 2-3 weeks — the ledger is the project, the model calls are glue
clone_cost.why: The walkthrough is ordinary orchestration over two APIs: extract, prioritise, research, judge, draft, cross-check, render a diff. What takes the time is the claim ledger — extracting claims reliably, keying them so a re-run recognises the same claim in a re-edited article, and the due-date and link graph on top — plus the fixture recorder that keeps iteration cheap. The dependency-free core design is what makes the second part cheap to get right.

audit.what_to_steal: Record fixtures on the first live run — write every search result and model response to disk once, and every later iteration is free; that single habit is what made the whole thing developable on a hackathon budget. Keep vendor SDKs at the edges around a dependency-free core so the interesting logic runs on a bare interpreter with no key. Schedule re-verification per claim with a last-checked and next-due time rather than per page, and keep a link graph between claims so an edit to one paragraph can be checked against its neighbours. And always hand back a diff with citations instead of writing to the system of record.
audit.what_breaks_first: The fixed staleness window. 'Skip what was verified last week' is a single guess about decay rates applied uniformly, and it is wrong in both directions for the facts this targets: a film's release date almost never moves, while 'current holder of X' can move in a day — so the budget is spent re-checking stable facts while the volatile ones age out between passes. Second: the reviewer's queue. 'Sources disagree' is a terminal category with no triage described, and on a long contested article it can hold a large share of the claims; a maintainer handed forty cited diffs and thirty unresolved disagreements has been given a new job, not a lighter one.

prior_art.relation: the same shape — a machine ranking facts for a human to act on, deliberately stopping short of acting — and the two pages differ almost entirely on whether the judgement is checkable: Continuity returns old text, new text, a citation and a confidence score per claim, while the fisheries tool returns a risk classification whose own page says there is no ground truth for it.

both convert an unverifiable judgement into an artifact a person can check (a cited diff, a signed finding) and both keep the human as the writer of record; the difference is what they attach evidence to — one grounds a claim against the live web on a schedule, the other against a versioned rule set in CI.

both are staged agent pipelines that publish a dollar figure, and read together they move the number worth tracking: Greenlight quotes cost per run against a measured output, Continuity quotes total build cost and explains that fixtures made every later iteration free — so iteration cost, not run cost, is what decides whether a pipeline is developable.

learnway-ai.name: LearnWay AI
learnway-ai.summary: An AI-native learning platform powered by Gemini that personalizes learning, provides AI mentorship, assesses real-world projects and helps people build practical, career-ready skills.

inspiration_intel.the_wedge: The team treated the annoying part of the workflow as the product, not the demo.
inspiration_intel.what_it_does: An AI-native learning platform powered by Gemini that personalizes learning, provides AI mentorship, assesses real-world projects and helps people build practical, career-ready skills.
steal_this: Steal the framing: Tutors & Adaptive Learning work inside Learning & Knowledge Systems, done as a bounded loop.
inspiration_intel.naive_version_vs_this: A demo that needs the user to already know what to type. — then LearnWay AI made the step measurable, gated, or priced instead.
inspiration_intel.reuse_surface: portable to any agent that touches production data

audit.worth_note: The geography is the idea. 'AI tutor plus mentor plus assessment' is the most common six-bullet pitch on this shelf - learnway's own competitors in this corpus are lumina-study-buddy, accomplish and antislop - and the page concedes that features are not the measure. What makes LearnWay worth a slot is that it is built for the constraint that breaks the others: phones on mobile data, low-cost devices, tutors who are unavailable at any price, and content that must be localised rather than translated. That is a real design brief and it is the reason this is `niche` and not `tired`. It stops there because not one claim about effect is falsifiable: the record asserts production apps, production AI and continuous improvement, and publishes no learner count, no completion rate, no grading comparison and no repository, while naming the right metric - whether learners achieve better outcomes - without reporting it. Publishing on the lite ladder says exactly that: the page establishes what the product is for and how it is wired, and cannot establish that it works.

artifact_exists.why: no source repo linked, but the page publishes a working artifact: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZvUzd7mBRbU

build_is_real.why: no repository published, so the build cannot be read

limits_disclosed.why: the team described how hard the build was, but not a limitation of the system itself — no accuracy, coverage, privacy or failure-mode statement

numbers_add_up.why: 1 figure(s) re-derived and reconcile (4 likes on Devpost), but 3 headline figure(s) carry no testable denominator: six AI capabilities and eight Built With tags; millions of people want into the digital economy

stack_consistency.why: no repo to cross-check the declared stack against

test_or_eval_evidence.why: the only testing sentence on the page is a denial (no suite, set or run is linked)

assumptions: the courses and progress state exist independently of the AI layer, since the page describes a pivot onto existing infrastructure rather than a new build
no model is trained or fine-tuned - every AI surface named is a hosted Gemini call - so quality rests on prompting and supplied learner context
translation is machine translation with AI assistance, as no human review or per-market authoring process is described
clone_cost.why: Reproducing the described surface is weeks, not days: a Flutter client for two platforms, NestJS over PostgreSQL with learner, course, progress and assessment schemas, four Gemini surfaces (tutor, mentor, quiz generation, feedback), translation wiring, plus the authoring workflow for course content. The months are in what the page does not describe and the market demands - a catalogue that is relevant per market rather than merely translated, grading that can be trusted enough to be called assessment, and an economics answer for inference on a learner's five-minute session over metered data.

what_to_steal: Put the model in the transition, not in a panel. The tutor fires while a learner is stuck mid-lesson, the mentor decides what comes next, the assessment closes the loop; the loop Learn -> Ask -> Practice -> Assess -> Feedback -> Improve -> Continue is the spec. A chatbot beside a video library has the same model and none of the leverage.

Design against the client the user owns, and say so as a constraint: smartphone-only, metered data, cheap hardware, intermittent connectivity. Most AI-edu pitches assume a laptop and a broadband connection and thereby address the learners who least need help.

Treat the pivot as a kept-and-added structure: LearnWay's courses, progress tracking and PostgreSQL state stayed, and the AI layer was built on top of them with that context as input. The alternative - a green-field AI app with no learner state - is why most education demos cannot personalise anything.

Bound the model's authority by the human you are not replacing: 'not to eliminate educators and mentors' is stated as the design objective, which is the honest version of the autonomy debate most records only gesture at.

Instrument the AI features as a first-class product surface - the page says usage and operational data are captured to see how learners interact with them. This is the one hook that could have produced an outcome number, and it is also the caution: telemetry about engagement is not evidence about learning.
what_breaks_first: AI-generated quizzes and assessment feedback, which is the capability the whole pivot claims most from and the one with the least published. A generated quiz tests recall of the lesson that was just shown, not whether the skill exists; a generated feedback sentence reads as coaching while grading against a rubric nobody wrote down. Because no accuracy figure, human comparison or rubric is published, there is no way to tell useful feedback from confident feedback - and in a credential-adjacent product that is the failure a learner pays for.

'AI-assisted content workflows' for authoring courses: five words carrying the quality of everything downstream. If generated material enters the library unreviewed, the platform's most important asset becomes unverifiable at the exact scale it is trying to reach, and localisation errors travel with it.

The multilingual claim as stated: Google Cloud Translation localises text, and the page concedes that relevance does not follow from translation. Machine-translated example sentences, currencies, units and cultural references are how a learning product loses credibility with the market it was built for, and no human review step is described anywhere.

Cost per learner at scale. Tutor, mentor, quiz generation and assessment feedback are four inference surfaces per learner per session on a metered-data phone in a market where the whole pitch is price; the page never states a per-learner cost, so the unit economics that decide whether this model survives outside a hackathon are entirely absent.

Deployment claims without an artifact: production Android and iOS apps and a production AI stack are asserted, and neither a store listing, a URL nor a repository is linked, so a reader cannot open what the record is built on. If the store apps are the pre-pivot LearnWay client and the AI layer is not yet shipped to it, the word 'production' is doing two jobs at once.

prior_art.relation: the same pitch at the other end of engineering effort, and the reason this batch is instructive: LearnWay has production clients, a Postgres state machine and four named AI surfaces; Antislop has a PySide shell and a prompt. Neither publishes a learning outcome, so the twelve-field ladder cannot separate them on effect - only the page-substance floor does, which is exactly the distinction the audited-lite tier was built to draw.

the direct competitor in this corpus for the same market, and it holds the answer LearnWay is missing. ax4u sells outputs instead of lessons - an automated workflow, a published book, a deployable system - so 'did the learner acquire a skill' is answered by a deliverable a third party can inspect. LearnWay's loop ends at 'receive feedback'. Read as a pair, the record with the weaker infrastructure has the stronger verification.

the same evidence shape in a different vertical, which is why the lite ladder exists: a shipped, monetised, multi-locale product whose load-bearing model claim is unpublished. Both list localisations as a feature and neither lists an accuracy or outcome figure for the model that the feature depends on.

an instruction that transfers. AttainDesk's year of SMB support work concluded 'less AI, not more'; LearnWay's page argues the opposite direction - AI operating the journey - while agreeing that features are not the measure. The pair frames the open question for every agent-shaped product in this catalog: who evaluates whether the added autonomy helped, and where does that evidence get published.
